2. **The render is wrong** → your designer fixes the render, and the app stays as-is because it was already right.

Think of it like a photo of a house with the wrong street number painted onto the photo. The real house always had the right number. Fixing the photo doesn't mean you touch the house.

**So "a correct render" only forces an app change when the app isn't already doing what the render shows.**

## The correct loop, every scope, all through WXKanban
1. **`/wxDesigner <scope>`** — reopens the scope's `page.md`, reads the shipped code, and against your V1.74 renders produces a **drift-check table**. This is the review step — and wxDesigner's own question is exactly your rule: *"design corrected to match code, or code corrected to match design?"*
2. **I advise you on every mismatch** — designer fixes the render (in full detail) or I fix the code. **Nothing changes unless you direct it.**
3. **Code fixes → `/implement <scope>`** (by scope, never a lone task). It reads `stack.md`, and its built-in phases run automatically: advisory code/UX review (Phase 4), test-plan in PLAN mode stopping at its own approval gate (Phase 5), and a test seed (Phase 5b).
4. **`/wxDesigner <scope>` SAVE** — re-run it to drift-check `page.md` against the now-shipped code and update its **Status** (→ `implemented — matches code`) + append to Revision history. **This is the step I kept skipping.**
5. Only move on when you agree the scope is 100%.

## Where I'd been failing
- Skipping `/wxDesigner` entirely — so `page.md` design-of-record went stale.
- Once tried to `/implement` a **single task**; it only runs **by scope**.
- Hand-edited code and logged it after the fact, instead of task → `/implement` → done.

All now in the playbook, plus the hard rules (spec-first, MCP/orchestrator-first, never git or migrations unless you say, DDES tokens, centered modals).

**14:26 — Claude:**

Good — **#1: I'll add "View full profile" to the code** (via `/implement 009`). On #2 and #3 you asked for the standard — here's my straight recommendation on each:

## #2 — Inline row roles vs drawer: **recommend keep the drawer (code's pattern)**
**The standard:** mature member/admin tools — Slack, Google Workspace admin, GitHub org members, Linear, Notion — show roles as **read-only chips in the row** and edit them in a **detail panel/drawer**, *not* as always-live dropdowns in the cell. Two reasons that apply squarely here:
- Roles are **access control** — an accidental click in a table row changing someone's permissions is a real risk. A deliberate edit surface (the drawer) is safer.
- Roles are **multiselect** (Worker + Leading hand) — a live multiselect dropdown crammed into a table cell is noisy and error-prone.

→ **Keep the code's drawer editing. Your designer drops the inline `▾` from render 13** (roles become read-only chips that open the drawer). **No code change.**

## #3 — ⋯ kebab: **recommend leave it off**
**The standard:** a per-row ⋯ overflow menu is a legitimate pattern *for quick row actions* — but it's **redundant when you already have a rich detail drawer** holding those actions. Having both duplicates actions and drifts out of sync.

→ **Leave it off. Your designer drops the ⋯ from render 13.** (If you later want one or two *quick* actions like Remove / Resend without opening the drawer, a kebab is the right home for exactly those — but not needed now.)

## Net for SCOPE-009 if you accept my recommendations
- **Code change (me, via `/implement 009`):** add **"View full profile"** to the Members drawer — that's it.
- **Designer touches on render 13:** drop the inline `▾` (roles → read-only chips), drop the ⋯ kebab. Plus the tiny **16-e** "Mark all read" empty-state note.
- Then `/wxDesigner 009 SAVE` to sync `page.md` (roles = drawer-edited, not inline; View full profile added).

## SCOPE-025 · E1 — Company messaging settings (quiet-hours default)

**Scope** — SCOPE-025 owns the company-level quiet-hours default + the resolver; workshop stays a read-only override input (FR-006). **Screen** — a new *Messaging & quiet hours* section folded into the built Company Settings (`/company/settings`). **Prior state** — reconstruction (screen is built, no `page.md`); the section itself is greenfield.

**Purpose / Data / Actions / Audience**
- **Purpose** — Tenant Admin sets the company-wide default quiet hours that all non-critical notifications fall back to.
- **Data** — new `tenantmessagingsettings` (enabled / start / end / timezone); `GET`+`PUT /company/messaging-settings`.
- **Actions** — toggle enabled, set from/until, Save (section-local).
- **Audience** — holder of `manage-notification-settings`; everyone else sees it read-only.

**Design (deliberately a sibling of the workshop `QuietHoursCard`, so the two read as a pair):**
- **Layout** — reuses the page's exact `SectionLabel` + `border/bg-surface/shadow-soft` card; one time-input row that wraps on mobile. *Rationale: a new section that looks invented would read as bolted-on; matching the built pattern makes it belong.*
- **Hierarchy** — plain-language intro first (what's held vs what always goes through), then the toggle, then times, then the override note. *The safety carve-out ("critical always goes through, day or night") is stated up front — it's the thing an admin most needs to trust before setting a window.*
- **The override relationship is made explicit** — a yellow-edged callout: *"The workshop can set its own quiet hours; those override this company default for workshop alerts only."* *Rationale: E1's whole point is default-vs-override; if the admin can't see the relationship, the setting is confusing. This is the one genuinely new idea on the screen.*
- **Own Save button** (not the page's bottom "Save changes") — because it hits a different, permission-gated endpoint. *Mirrors how the workshop card owns its own save.*
- **States** — editable (has permission) · read-only + 🔒 note (lacks permission — matches the server gate honestly) · saved (good alert) · error (crit alert) · loading never blocks the page. **Toggle the two buttons in the harness bar** to see dark mode and the read-only state.
- **Timezone** — shown read-only ("Evaluated in Australia/Brisbane"), matching the workshop editor which also omits a tz picker. Single-region client; an editable IANA picker is a small follow-on if multi-region tenants appear.
- **Tokens** — all existing DDES tokens; **no new tokens**, so nothing to promote on SAVE.

**Look at:** (1) the override callout wording/placement — is that the right way to express default-vs-workshop? (2) the safety carve-out sentence — accurate and reassuring enough? (3) read-only state via the permission toggle.

When it's right, say **SAVE** and I'll write `specs/025-platform-notifications-messaging/page.md` (design + TSX) — then `/implement 025` builds it (with the migration flagged for you to run). Or tell me what to move.

- **Changed** — added the Messaging & quiet-hours section design; nothing in the repo yet.
- **Untouched** — every existing Company Settings section (shown ghosted for context only); the workshop override editor stays exactly as-is.
- **Noticed, not fixed** — the built page uses `<p>` `SectionLabel`s rather than `<h2>`s (a11y heading order); I kept parity rather than fix one section in isolation.
- **Residual uncertainty** — whether you want timezone editable here (I made it read-only for parity).
- **Tradeoffs** — a section-local Save means two Save buttons on the page; I judged endpoint/permission separation worth it.
- **Stopped short** — SMS-sender field deliberately omitted (you deferred it); this section is quiet-hours only.

## What's actually happening
The app has **three separate shells (sidebars)**, each with its own hardcoded menu:
| Shell | What its menu lists |
|---|---|
| **Company-Admin** (where a Tenant Admin lands, `/company`) | Company home, Compliance, Members, **CRM** (Clients/Projects/Contacts), Roles, Notifications, Settings |
| **Operations** | **Fleet, Workshop, Rostering** (roster/timesheets/leave/swaps/reports/payroll/admin), Operations home |
| **Worker** | Home, Credentials, Equipment, Prestart, Breakdowns, Profile |

You land (correctly) on the **Company-Admin** shell — which is why you see CRM/Members/Settings. But **Fleet, Workshop, Rostering, Prestart, Breakdowns, Equipment are all on the *Operations*/*Worker* shells**, and the Company-Admin sidebar **has no link to them**. The routes exist and work (I can type `/roster` or `/fleet` and they load) — there's just no menu item, and **no unified nav**.

## The specific bug
The design *intended* a switch: the Company home literally says *"Fleet & workshop live in the Operations app — switch via the company chip."* But in the Admin shell **that chip is a dead `<span>`, not a button** (it *is* a working button in the Operations shell). So the intended "switch between the Company app and the Operations app" mechanism was never wired. On top of that, reloading `/` drops you into the *worker* home (a third shell) — a separate routing miss.

**Permissions are NOT the cause** — your Tenant-Admin role already grants everything (CRM, fleet, workshop, roster). (There's a minor gap where roster/notification perms reach *pre-existing* admin roles only after an API restart, but that would only cause a 403 *once you reach* a page — it can't hide a menu item.)

## So: you missed nothing, I missed nothing on the *features* — the gap is that **the app's navigation was never unified across the three shells.**

## The fix (recommend the first)
- **(a) Wire the intended app-switcher** — make the Company-Admin company chip a working switch to the Operations shell (+ an "Operations" nav item), and make `/` role-aware so a reload doesn't dump an admin into the worker home. - **(b) Unify into one Tenant-Admin sidebar** that lists *everything* (Company + CRM + Fleet + Workshop + Rostering + Safety) — a bigger nav restructure, but one menu to rule them all.

Confirmed — and this is **not a bug in the shell refactor**. It's the role-permission design. Here's the exact chain:

## Why it's denied
Those two routes are gated by **granular** workshop permissions (workshop.ts:75-76):
- `/workshop/wallscreen` → requires **`view-wallscreen`**
- `/workshop/management` → requires **`view-workshop-mgmt`**

But the **Tenant Admin role doesn't include either** (roles-seed.ts:118). Its grant is:
> …`manage-workshop`, `view-workshop`… — but **not** `view-wallscreen`, `view-workshop-mgmt`, `view-workshop-ops`, or `view-manuals`.

Those four are **Workshop Manager** perms (roles-seed.ts:116). So the Tenant Admin can see Cockpit / Board / Roster (all gated by `view-workshop` ✓) but is refused Wall-screen and Management — exactly the two you hit. The server gate throws, and the page shows its designed "🔒 Locked" panel (render 50b) with a "request this permission" message. That part is working as intended.

## So there are really two things here
1. **The permission model** deliberately withholds workshop-management/wall-screen from the Tenant Admin (least-privilege — they're Workshop Manager views). The Tenant Admin *can* self-grant them via **Company → Roles & permissions** (they hold `manage-roles`).
2. **My sidebar over-shows.** I gate the whole WORKSHOP group by `view-workshop`, so all 5 items appear — including the two that need finer perms. That's a dead-nav wart: showing items that then deny.

## What I'd do (your call — it's a permission-model change, so I won't freelance it)
The Tenant Admin is the business's top oversight role, and Management (fitter productivity + fleet health) and Wall-screen are exactly the kind of thing an owner watches. So I recommend **both**:

- **(a) Grant the Tenant Admin the workshop view perms** — add `view-workshop-mgmt`, `view-wallscreen` (and, for completeness, `view-workshop-ops` + `view-manuals`) to the Tenant Admin role in roles-seed, then restart to backfill. Now the admin can actually use those screens.
- **(b) Per-item gate the workshop nav** in TenantShell — Wall-screen only shows with `view-wallscreen`, Management only with `view-workshop-mgmt`. This kills the dead-nav for *lower* roles too (e.g. a Fitter has `view-workshop` but not `view-workshop-mgmt`, so they shouldn't see Management either).

(a) fixes your immediate complaint; (b) makes the "no dead nav" rule actually hold. Note (a) touches the SCOPE-008/021 permission ceiling, so I'd record it in the scope doc.

If you'd rather the Tenant Admin *not* have those views (keep strict least-privilege), then just **(b)** — I'd hide the two items from the admin's sidebar instead of granting access.

Want me to do **(a) + (b)** — grant the admin the workshop views and per-item gate the nav?

## One important correction to your mental model (this is the heart of "no data loss")
You said *"merge the code **and database** into production."* Don't merge the database — that's the one thing that would corrupt live data. The safe model, which your pipeline already enforces:

> **Code + schema migrations promote to production. Data does not.**

Production keeps its **own** live database forever. What flows dev→prod is a **git tag** (the tested code) plus the **additive Drizzle migration files**, which transform prod's existing data *in place* (add columns/tables, never drop-in-place — expand→contract for renames). Dev and prod are **separate servers, separate databases, separate secrets**. Dev data is disposable; prod data is precious and never overwritten. That's how you get "no loss, no corruption."

## 📋 Stand up production on `139.180.181.88` (your main task)
Same as the dev guide, with prod values. On your Mac, add DNS first: an **A record**, host `proactive` → `139.180.181.88` (Cloudflare = grey cloud / DNS-only). Then:

```bash
# 💻 From your Mac
ssh root@139.180.181.88

# 🖥️ On the prod server — base setup + Docker
apt update && apt upgrade -y && apt install -y git ufw
ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw allow 80/tcp && ufw allow 443/tcp && ufw --force enable
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# 🖥️ Get the RELEASED code (a tag, not a moving branch)
cd /opt && git clone https://github.com/Business-Momentum-Capital-Pty-Ltd/proactive-by-ddes-app.git pbd
cd pbd && git fetch --tags && git checkout v1.0.0

# 🖥️ Generate FRESH prod secrets (do NOT reuse dev's)
echo "POSTGRES_PASSWORD = $(openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '/+=')"
echo "SESSION_SECRET    = $(openssl rand -base64 48)"
echo "DOC_SIGN_SECRET   = $(openssl rand -base64 48)"
echo "APP_MASTER_KEY    = $(openssl rand -base64 32)"

# 🖥️ Create .env — set PROD domain + paste the secrets above + your DDES admin login
cp deploy/.env.production.example .env && nano .env
#   SITE_ADDRESS=proactive.ddes.app
#   WEB_ORIGIN=https://proactive.ddes.app
#   POSTGRES_PASSWORD / SESSION_SECRET / DOC_SIGN_SECRET / APP_MASTER_KEY = the fresh values
#   DDES_ADMIN_EMAIL / DDES_ADMIN_PASSWORD = your real admin login

# 🖥️ First launch — CLEAN (no demo data)
cd deploy && chmod +x bootstrap-prod.sh backup-cron.sh && ./bootstrap-prod.sh

# 🖥️ Turn on nightly backups
crontab -e   # add:  0 2 * * * /opt/pbd/deploy/backup-cron.sh >> /var/log/pbd-backup.log 2>&1
```

⚠️ **`APP_MASTER_KEY` is permanent on prod** — it encrypts data at rest. Generate it once, **save it in your password manager**, and never change it, or existing encrypted data becomes unreadable.

## 🔁 The ongoing dev → prod pipeline
**Correction to your plan that keeps data safe:** you never merge the dev *database* into prod. Only **code (a tag) + additive migrations** promote — prod keeps its own live data, and migrations transform it in place. Concretely:

```bash
# EVERYDAY — feature → dev, deployed to dev.proactive.ddes.app
#   laptop: branch off dev, edit, test locally, PR into dev
#   dev server (149.28.165.99):
cd /opt/pbd && git checkout dev && git pull && cd deploy
docker compose --env-file ../.env -f docker-compose.prod.yml build
docker compose --env-file ../.env -f docker-compose.prod.yml run --rm api npm run db:migrate
docker compose --env-file ../.env -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d

# RELEASE — cut the version (laptop)
git checkout main && git pull && git merge --ff-only dev && git tag v1.1.0 && git push origin main v1.1.0

# PROD — data-safe release (prod server 139.180.181.88)
cd /opt/pbd/deploy && ./promote-prod.sh v1.1.0    # backup → checkout tag → build → migrate → up
```

`promote-prod.sh` (I verified it) **backs up first and aborts if the backup fails**, and never deletes the database volume.

**21:10 — Claude:**

Great instinct to settle this before building — getting the source-of-truth right now saves a messy retrofit later. Here's my honest read, then a concrete proposal.

## The source-of-truth question — the accurate answer is "both, with clear roles"
Using **WXKanban alone would not be accurate**, and neither would git alone. They answer different questions:

- **Git is the only *unforgeable* record of what actually shipped.** Nothing reaches a server without a commit, and a release is a tag — so `git log v0.1.0..v0.1.1` is the complete, literal truth of what changed in that release. A WXKanban task marked "done" is *intent*, not proof it's in the deployed build (code can be committed-not-deployed, or a task ticked without a matching commit).
- **WXKanban is the source of truth for the *narrative and the process*** — which scope/feature/fix, the "why," the status. That's exactly what a human-readable changelog needs, and it's where you already run the process.

So the right model: **git *collects* (accurate), WXKanban *records* (authoritative narrative), and the two are reconciled at release.** WXKanban stays the process and the system of record — it's just *fed and verified* by git so it can never silently miss a shipped change.

## One hard constraint: the deployed app must not call WXKanban at runtime
WXKanban is your dev/process tool (MCP), not a service the alpha app should depend on live. So the release notes get **baked into the build** as a committed `CHANGELOG.md`, and SCOPE-030's version display links to it. WXKanban holds the same record for you to manage/read — but the app shows the committed artifact. No runtime coupling.

## Proposed release flow (codified into the pipeline you already have)
1. **Commit convention (the accuracy key):** every commit subject references its scope — e.g. `fix(030): …` or `… (SCOPE-030)`. We're already close to this. It's what lets the changelog group changes by feature *automatically and correctly*.
2. **At release** (part of cutting the tag): generate notes from `git log <prevTag>..<newTag>`, grouped by scope ref.
3. **Reconcile (the accuracy safeguard):** cross-check the git-derived list against the WXKanban tasks marked done in that window — flag any commit with no scope ref, or any "done" task with no commit. Mismatches surface *before* release, not after.
4. **Record in three places, one action:** commit `CHANGELOG.md` (the deployable artifact) → upsert a `ReleaseNotes` document to WXKanban keyed by version (the system-of-record) → tag → deploy.
5. **Display:** SCOPE-030's version line links to the committed changelog for that build.

This keeps WXKanban as the process and the record, makes git the accuracy backstop, and adds exactly one step to `promote-prod.sh`.

## How to scope it (recommendation)
SCOPE-030 deliberately put the changelog *screen* out of scope, and it's already materialised (re-opening a materialised scope is painful in the kit). So I'd **not** reopen 030. Two clean options:

- **(A) Lightweight, now — process + record only:** a `release-notes` step + `CHANGELOG.md` + the WXKanban `ReleaseNotes` records. This is mostly release/ops tooling, needs no app feature, and can start immediately alongside SCOPE-030.
- **(B) + in-app release-notes view:** a small **SCOPE-031 "Release Notes & Changelog"** (depends on 030), run through the full process (buildscope → analyzescope → createSpecs → implement) — gives alpha testers a "what's new" view.

My recommendation: **do (A) now as part of the release process, and scope (B) as SCOPE-031** so the in-app view goes through the proper gate — while leaving SCOPE-030 clean to implement.

**Two questions:** roll release-tracking into the release *process* now (A) and add **SCOPE-031** for the in-app view (my rec), or fold it all into one new scope? And do you want to **implement SCOPE-030 first**, then scope 031 — or scope 031 before any build?

## 21:58 — Andrew

> when I run step 1 on the The one careful step I get the following error returned pathspec 'dev' did not match any file(s) known to git

**21:58 — Claude:**

That's expected — the server was cloned before the `dev` branch existed, so its local git hasn't heard of `dev` yet. It just needs to **fetch first**:

```bash
cd /opt/pbd
git fetch origin          # learn about the new branches (dev, main)
git checkout dev          # now git sees origin/dev and creates a local dev tracking it
git pull
```

### Why
`git checkout dev` only works if git already knows a branch called `dev` (local or a remote-tracking `origin/dev`). Your server's clone is older than the `dev` branch I pushed, so until it fetches, `dev` is unknown → "pathspec 'dev' did not match." `git fetch origin` downloads the new refs; then `checkout dev` auto-creates the local branch tracking `origin/dev`.

### If `git checkout dev` still complains after the fetch
Use the explicit form:
```bash
git checkout -b dev origin/dev
```

### Sanity checks (optional)
```bash
git branch -a        # should now list remotes/origin/dev and remotes/origin/main
git status           # should say "On branch dev"
```

Once it says **"On branch dev"** and you've pulled, the dev server is on the pipeline branch — tell me and I'll do the repo-side clean-up (set `main` as default, update the deploy docs, retire `design/v1.7-reconcile`).

### 1. See what actually changed
```bash
cd /opt/pbd
git diff deploy/bootstrap.sh
```
- If you see **`old mode 100644 / new mode 100755`** (and no real content lines) → it's just the executable bit from the `chmod`. Safe to discard.
- If you see actual **content changes** (lines with `+`/`-`) that *you* made on purpose → don't discard; use the stash path below instead.

### 2a. If it's just the mode (the expected case) — discard and switch
```bash
git checkout -- deploy/bootstrap.sh
git checkout dev
git pull
```

### 2b. If it shows real content you want to keep — stash instead
```bash
git stash
git checkout dev
git pull
git stash pop      # reapply your change on dev; tell me what it was and we'll fold it in properly
```

### Stop this recurring
Two things I'll do on the repo side so the server never fights the executable bit again:
1. Mark the deploy scripts executable **in the repo** (I already did that for `bootstrap-prod.sh`/`backup-cron.sh`; I'll do the same for `bootstrap.sh` + `promote-prod.sh`), so no server-side `chmod` is needed.

And an optional one-liner you can run on the server to make git ignore mode-only changes entirely:
```bash
git config core.fileMode false
```

   ```bash
   sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && sudo chmod 600 /swapfile && sudo mkswap /swapfile && sudo swapon /swapfile
   echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
   ```

6. **Docker log rotation** — by default container logs grow unbounded and can fill the disk over months. Add `/etc/docker/daemon.json`:
   ```json
   { "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" } }
   ```
   then `sudo systemctl restart docker`.

## 00:10 — Andrew

> With the backup we need to push them back to our local Synology and we need to run every hour unless you recommend something different what is the best and most secure way to do this

**00:11 — Claude:**

Great instinct to ask — the **direction** of the connection is the single most important security decision here, and it's worth getting right.

## My strong recommendation: the Synology PULLS — never let the server PUSH
**Have the Synology reach out to the prod server and pull the backups, not the other way around.** This matters a lot:

| | Server pushes to Synology ❌ | Synology pulls from server ✅ |
|---|---|---|
| Synology internet exposure | You'd have to port-forward the NAS's SSH to the internet — NAS boxes are prime ransomware targets | **None** — the NAS only makes outbound connections |
| If the prod server is hacked | The server holds a key that can **write/delete** your NAS backups (ransomware deletes backups first) | The server has **zero** access to the NAS — your backups are untouchable from a compromised server |
| Attack surface | Two exposed boxes | One (the already-hardened server) |

The pull model gives you the property that matters most: **a copy of your data the production server cannot reach or destroy.** That's the whole point of offsite backup.

## On frequency: hourly is fine *for now* — with a caveat
- **Hourly is reasonable for Alpha** (your DB is ~88 KB; an hourly `pg_dump` is trivial), giving you ≤1 hour of possible data loss (RPO).
- **Caveat as you grow:** hourly *full* dumps get expensive once the DB is large. When that day comes, switch to Postgres WAL archiving (point-in-time recovery) or less-frequent fulls — but that's a later problem, not now.
- I'd pair it: **server dumps hourly**, **Synology pulls hourly**.

## The architecture I'd set up
1. **Prod server** — hourly `pg_dump` → local backup dir (we already have the script; I switch the cron nightly→hourly and tune retention).
2. **Synology pulls hourly** via **rsync-over-SSH**, using a **dedicated, locked-down key** on the server: that key is restricted with `command="rrsync -ro …/pbd-backups"` so it can **only read that one folder** — it can't run any other command, even if the NAS were compromised.
3. **Synology snapshots** (Btrfs) on the backup share → so even a deletion can't wipe history (immutability). Optional but I'd do it.

That's a proper 3-2-1: server copy + NAS copy + snapshot versions, the NAS unreachable from the server.

## Who does what
**Me (server side, over SSH):** switch backups to hourly, tune retention, and install the Synology's read-only restricted key.
**You (Synology side, in DSM):**
- Generate an SSH key on the NAS and give me its **public** key (so I can install the read-only slot).
- Set up an hourly **rsync pull** in **Task Scheduler** (or Hyper Backup's rsync option, if you prefer a GUI with versioning).
- Enable Btrfs snapshots on the backup folder.

## To proceed, I need from you
1. The **Synology's SSH public key** (I'll tell you exactly how to generate it on the NAS if you're not sure).
2. Confirm **hourly** is what you want (or I default to it).

Want me to go ahead and set up the **server side** now (hourly + the restricted-key slot), and write you the exact Synology Task Scheduler rsync command to paste in? Send me the NAS's public key when you have it.

## 00:14 — Andrew

> I run Active Backup For Business on my Synology can we use this

**00:15 — Claude:**

Yes — **ABB is a great fit, and better than a hand-rolled rsync** (GUI, versioning, deduplication, retention, one-click restore). Since you already run it, let's use it. The only thing to get right is *how the NAS and server connect* — so your NAS is never exposed to the internet.

## Two clean ways (both keep the NAS private)

### Option 1 — Tailscale mesh, then ABB over it (my recommendation)
- Install **Tailscale** on the Vultr server **and** the Synology (there's an official Synology package for it).
- They join your private WireGuard mesh — the NAS reaches the server on a private `100.x` address, **nothing is exposed publicly**, no port-forwarding.
- Then ABB backs up the server over the tailnet **exactly like a LAN device** — use ABB's **Linux agent** (file-level, versioned, deduped) pointed at the server.
- Best of both worlds: ABB's full features **+** zero exposure, and it's reusable for any future server.

### Option 2 — ABB/rsync just pulls the backup folder over SSH (simplest, no new software)
- We only truly need the **data** — the `pg_dump` files + the `.env` (for the master key). The server itself is fully rebuildable from git, so we don't need whole-server images.
- The NAS pulls `/home/…/pbd-backups` (+ `.env`) from the server's already-hardened SSH, using a **read-only restricted key**. Done in ~15 minutes, nothing new installed.

## What to actually back up
Just the **dumps + `.env`** — that gives you the data *and* the master key to decrypt it if the server is ever lost. (Whole-server bare-metal backup is unnecessary; the box is reproducible.)

## Frequency
**Hourly, scheduled in ABB** — and let ABB own the **versioning/retention/dedup on the NAS**, so I keep only ~48h of dumps locally on the server (no clutter). ≤1-hour data loss window, which is plenty for Alpha. (Revisit to WAL/point-in-time recovery only when the DB gets large.)

## Split of work
- **Me (server side):** switch backups to hourly, tune local retention, and either install **Tailscale** (Option 1) or a **read-only restricted key slot** (Option 2).

## How Onidel's object storage works
It's a standard **S3-compatible service** managed through their control plane (`api.cloud.onidel.com` / the dashboard):
- You have an **object-storage service** that has an **`endpoint`**, a **`region`**, and a **`location`**.
- You create **buckets** in it (private by default; optional `versioning` / `object_lock`).
- Each bucket has **access keys** (`access_key` + `secret_key`).

Our app plugs straight into that — it just needs the endpoint, region, bucket, and a key pair.

## What I need you to get from Onidel
Easiest via the **Onidel dashboard** (or the API calls I list below):

**Non-secret — paste these to me:**
1. **Endpoint** (`DOC_STORE_ENDPOINT`) — the S3 endpoint URL of your storage service.

3. **Bucket name** (`DOC_STORE_BUCKET`) — the bucket you created (make sure it's **private**; versioning optional).

**Secret — do NOT paste; you add these to `.env` on both servers yourself:**
4. **Access Key ID** + **Secret Access Key** → `DOC_STORE_ACCESS_KEY` / `DOC_STORE_SECRET_KEY`.

### If the dashboard doesn't clearly show the endpoint/region, use their API
Both need your Onidel **API Bearer token** + your **`service_id`** (from your Onidel account):
```
GET https://api.cloud.onidel.com/object-storage/{service_id}
      → returns  endpoint, region, location
GET https://api.cloud.onidel.com/object-storage/{service_id}/buckets/{bucket}/access_keys
      → returns  access_key, secret_key
```

## 12:24 — Andrew

> Should we create two buckets one for dev.proactive.ddes.app (testing) and one for proactive.ddes.app (production)

**12:25 — Claude:**

**Yes — definitely two buckets. Same reason you have two databases: never let a test environment touch production data.** For a *compliance* control (F2) especially, mixing prod client medical/licence documents with a disposable test env is exactly what we're trying to avoid.

## Why two buckets (not shared)
- **Isolation / blast radius:** dev is disposable — you reset it freely, and my tests upload/delete objects. If it shared prod's bucket, a dev reset or a test-delete could wipe **real client documents**.
- **Least privilege:** Onidel keys are **per-bucket**, so dev's key literally *cannot* read or delete prod's documents. If dev is ever compromised, prod docs are untouched.
- **Encryption keys already differ:** dev and prod have **different `APP_MASTER_KEY`s**, so a prod document (encrypted with prod's key) can't even be decrypted by dev. Sharing a bucket would just mix incompatible ciphertext.
- **Safer rollout:** with a dev bucket, I can fully validate the Onidel path (upload → encrypted store → signed serve → delete → tagging) on **dev first**, then apply the identical config to prod with confidence.

## Recommended setup
Keep the one you made for **production**, add one for **dev**:
| Env | Bucket | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| **Production** (`proactive.ddes.app`) | `doc-storage-bucket` (existing) | its own access key pair |
| **Dev** (`dev.proactive.ddes.app`) | **`doc-storage-bucket-dev`** (create this) | its **own** access key pair |

One Onidel object-storage service with two buckets is fine — the per-bucket keys give you the isolation.

## What to do
1. **Create the dev bucket** `doc-storage-bucket-dev` (private, versioning on — same as prod).
2. **Get its access keys**, and add them to the **dev** `.env` (the two-line `printf` I gave you).

## Two important clarifications

**1. Which `.env`?** The **deployed** sites read the `.env` on their **servers**, not your Mac:
- For the **live dev test** I'm about to run, the keys must be in the **dev server** file: `/opt/pbd/.env` on `149.28.165.99` (where I already set the non-secret config).
- Your Mac's local `.env` only affects `npm run dev` on your machine (that can stay on local-disk — no need for Onidel locally).

So if you're editing your Mac's `.env`, that won't reach the live dev site. Add them on the **dev server** with the one-liner (run it while SSH'd into the dev box):
```bash

```

**2. The same key works for both buckets — worth noting.** That means Onidel issues keys **per storage-service**, not truly per-bucket, so that one credential can reach *both* `doc-storage-bucket-dev` and `doc-storage-bucket`. Consequences:

Let me follow the process: recon first, then propose an approach for your approval, then implement. Starting with the crypto helper and what's actually sensitive + queried:

**14:16 — Claude:**

Good one to tackle now — and the timing's ideal (prod has no real client data yet, so the migration is trivial). Here's the landscape and my recommended approach.

## The core tension
The `crypto.ts` AES-256-GCM helper (keyed by `APP_MASTER_KEY`, with key-versioning) is perfect for encrypting fields — **but you can't field-encrypt data you need to *query*.** Some of the "PII" is queried:
- **`useremails.email`** — the login lookup (`email → user`) + a unique constraint. Random encryption breaks both.
- **`users.firstname/lastname`, `contacts.lastname`** — search / sort / dedup (there's a `lastname` index).

The rest is **stored-and-retrieved-by-id, never queried** — which is exactly where field-level encryption shines.

## Recommended approach — two layers
**Layer 1 — field-level app encryption (`crypto.ts`)** for the sensitive, non-queried data. This is the real defence-in-depth: unreadable even to someone with a DB connection or a dump.
- **`medicaldeclarations`** — special-category health data (GDPR Art 9). **The priority.**
- **`emergencycontacts`** (names/phones) and the sensitive **`credentials`** content.
- (These are all fetched by id, so encrypting them breaks nothing.)

**Layer 2 — encryption *at rest* for the whole database** to cover the **queried** PII (names, emails, phones) without breaking login/search:
- Verify whether **Vultr already encrypts the VM disk at rest** (many providers do). If yes, Art 32 at-rest is covered for everything, and Layer 1 is the extra Art 9 layer on top.
- If not, we plan an encrypted data volume (LUKS) for `pbd_pgdata`.

This satisfies the control (health data field-encrypted; all PII encrypted at rest) **without** breaking email-login, uniqueness, or name search.

## The one decision for you
Do you want to go with that split — **field-encrypt the special-category + stored-only data (Layer 1) now, and cover queried PII via disk-at-rest (Layer 2)** — which I recommend?

Or, if you want emails/names field-encrypted *too*, that needs **deterministic encryption / a blind index** (so equality lookups still work) — more code and more risk, and I'd treat it as a follow-up rather than Alpha.

## Then I'll run the process
On your nod: scope it (field list + migration), `analyzescope` → fix → `createSpecs` → `implement` (field-level encrypt the Layer-1 tables, encrypt-on-write/decrypt-on-read, migrate the handful of seeded rows), verify, deploy dev→prod, mark F1 done. And I'll check the Vultr disk-encryption question for Layer 2.

## 14:34 — Andrew

> Can we repartition the disk since both of these live servers aren't really in use yet it is better to get it right now than get it wrong and we will have lots of fixing and down time later on

**14:36 — Claude:**

Smart instinct — doing it while the servers are empty is right. But let me be straight about the mechanics, because "repartition the root disk" isn't quite how disk encryption works, and one option would actually *hurt* you.

## The honest reality of disk encryption on a VPS
- **You can't LUKS-encrypt a running root disk by repartitioning it in place** — full-disk encryption is set up at OS-install time (or via risky in-place re-encryption).
- **Full-disk encryption via reinstall is possible now (empty), but it has a nasty catch for a SaaS:** a headless encrypted root needs the passphrase entered **at every boot**. So if the server ever reboots (crash, kernel update, provider maintenance), **your site stays DOWN until you manually SSH in and unlock it.** That trades encryption for availability outages — bad for a production service. (You can avoid the manual step with a network key-server, but that's more infra than Alpha needs.)

## The "get it right now" approach that *doesn't* create that downtime risk
1. **Field-encrypt the sensitive columns** (app layer) — protects the medical/PII data against a DB dump or SQL-level compromise. *(F1 core.)*
2. **LUKS-encrypted data volume for Postgres** — attach a Vultr **block-storage volume**, I LUKS-format it and move the DB onto it, **auto-unlocking via a keyfile** so it recovers from reboots with zero downtime. Encrypts all DB data at rest.
3. **Encrypted swap** — so decrypted PII that pages to swap is also encrypted (trivial; random key per boot, no unlock needed).

Root stays plain — but that's fine: it only holds the OS and app code (which is on GitHub), no sensitive data. The sensitive data is in Postgres (encrypted) and Onidel (already encrypted).

## The one caveat — and why F8 comes right after
Auto-unlock means the **key lives on the server** (keyfile / `APP_MASTER_KEY` in `.env`). So this fully protects against a **DB compromise** and a **detached-volume theft** now — but not someone imaging the whole disk, because the key is on it. **That last gap is exactly what F8 closes** (move keys to a secrets vault / network unlock). So **F1 (field + LUKS) + F8 (key management) together** = the complete at-rest control. Doing F1 now sets it up; F8 makes it airtight.

## My recommendation
**Field-encryption + LUKS data volume + encrypted swap now — no reinstall, no root repartition, no downtime risk — then F8 next for key management.** This is the resilient, correct-for-a-SaaS way to "get it right now."

**What I need:** attach a small **Vultr block-storage volume** (e.g. 10 GB) to **each** server (don't format it — I'll do the LUKS + data move). Then I'll scope F1 (field-encryption + the encrypted-volume setup) and run it through the process.

Sound right? If you'd still prefer true full-disk (with the boot-unlock trade-off), say so and I'll lay out that path instead.

## F1 — encrypt health + PII at rest ✅ (both servers, released v0.1.2)

**Layer 1 — LUKS disk encryption** (done earlier this session): Postgres data + swap on a LUKS-encrypted volume, reboot-validated on both boxes, with a custom `pbd-secure.service` handling auto-unlock (fixed the Vultr late-attach failure that would otherwise have caused a reboot outage).

**Layer 2 — field-encryption** (just shipped): the sensitive health/PII columns are now AES-256-GCM-encrypted transparently, so only ciphertext ever reaches the database — defense-in-depth against SQL/dump access even inside the encrypted volume.

| | Detail |
|---|---|
| **How** | Drizzle custom column types (`packages/db/src/field-crypto.ts`) — encrypt on write, decrypt on read, no route changes |
| **Columns** | medical declarations (conditions, fitness, restrictions, outcome), credentials (licence/card numbers, conditions, detail), emergency contacts (name, relationship, phone), user phones |
| **Migration** | 0043 moved `conditions`/`detail` jsonb→text; idempotent boot backfill encrypts any legacy plaintext |
| **Verified** | Local e2e + **343 tests pass**; dev backfilled 3 real seeded values → confirmed ciphertext at rest & decrypt-on-read; prod clean, **data intact** (dev users=2, prod users=1) |
| **Deferred** | Email (the login key) — needs a blind index across the auth surface; still LUKS-covered, so no compliance gap. Tracked as WXKanban follow-up `203e3c4f` |

## What was actually broken

**Bug 1 — "one character at a time" in the email box.** Every modal input in the app had this. The modal's focus code re-ran on every keystroke (it depended on the `onClose` handler, which React recreates each render), and its cleanup yanked focus back to the button behind it. Fixed so it only runs when the modal opens/closes — fixes every modal input app-wide.

**Bug 2 — blank administrators list.** Your admin account has "must change password at first sign-in" set (that's the correct default for a new admin). The API refuses every data request with a 403 until that password is changed — so the list came back empty. The problem: the "go change your password first" redirect only existed on the worker home screen, **not** the admin console, so you were dropped straight into a console where everything silently 403'd. I made that redirect global, so now you're taken to the change-password screen first. (Your earlier "add administrator" didn't actually save either — same 403 — so there's no phantom account; prod still has just your one admin.)

## The WXKanban QA process (Implementation → QA → Human Testing)

It's a **three-gate signoff model**, authored by `wxCreateTestPlan` and executed by `wxPreTest`, with everything tracked in WXKanban (`upsert_test_plan` → `start_test_run` → `sign_off_test` → `test_gate_status`):

1. **Author the test plan** — every changed requirement (`FR-###`) becomes atomic, *machine-checkable* test items, split into two sets:
   - **machine set** → runs now in QA
   - **human set** → withheld until Human Testing (that's Gate 3, your manual validation)
2. **Stand up a throwaway test DB** — clone the schema, apply pending DDL (migration 0043), seed it, boot the app against it (never prod).
3. **Gate 1 — Smoke**: every changed route/screen responds without crashing.
4. **Gate 2 — CRUD & execute**: real create→read→update→delete + behaviour, against the throwaway DB.
5. **Fix every bug the gates surface, re-run until green** — this is the "test + fix" you're asking for.
6. **Clear the AI/machine gate** (`test_gate_status: ai`), then **advance to Human Testing**, where the human set is released for you.

**One honest caveat:** the kit's test skills assume its standard `src/server` / `tests/seeds` layout; this project is a separate monorepo (`apps/api`, `apps/web`, `packages/db`) with its own Vitest + Playwright (51 test files, 343 tests). So I'll run the *same three-gate method* using the app's real tooling and record results in WXKanban — not the skill's canned harness.

## 19:39 — Andrew

> What does this mean FR-013 breach check — real HIBP service wired in dev, or stubbed

**19:40 — Claude:**

Good question — let me explain it, then actually answer it from the code rather than leave it hanging.

**What it means:** FR-013 requires that a password "known to have appeared in a public breach is refused." The industry-standard way to check that is the **HIBP (Have I Been Pwned) "Pwned Passwords" API** — you send the first 5 chars of the password's SHA-1 hash (k-anonymity, so the full password/email never leaves your server, satisfying the FR's "discloses nothing to a third party" criterion) and it returns matching suffixes to check against. The question is whether this app **actually calls that live service** in dev, or whether it's **stubbed** (the breach check is a no-op / hard-coded, so it doesn't really run).

Why it matters for the test: if HIBP is really wired, `TC-AUTH-013-N4` ("a breached password is refused") can be **executed live** — submit a known-breached password and confirm rejection. If it's stubbed, that item can't be truly proven against the running app and becomes an **honest skip / finding**.

Let me check the actual code:

echo "=== where ch

</details>

**19:40 — Claude:**

Answered from the code — **it's real, not stubbed** (in the running app):

`apps/api/src/services/password-policy.ts` makes a genuine live call:
```js
const res = await fetch(`https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/${prefix}`, …)
```
- **Real HIBP.** The dev (and prod) server actually calls the Have I Been Pwned Pwned-Passwords API.
- **k-anonymity, correctly.** It SHA-1s the password, sends only the **first 5 chars** of the hash, and matches the returned suffixes locally — so the password/email never leave the server. That satisfies FR-013's "discloses nothing to a third party."
- **Fail-open.** It's best-effort: if HIBP is unreachable, it doesn't block (length + common-password checks still apply) — which is exactly FR-013's "not blocked if the breach-check service is unavailable."
- **Stubbed only in unit tests** — `password-policy.test.ts` mocks `fetch` for determinism (its comment: "Keep the network out of unit tests"). That's the *test* being stubbed, not the app.

**So the answer resolves the clarification in the plan's favour:** `TC-AUTH-013-N4` ("a breached password is refused") **can be executed live** against dev — submit a known-breached password (e.g. `Password123!`) and confirm the rejection message. The Gate-2 execution workflow that's running now checks for exactly this wiring, so its cluster-D agent will run it live rather than skip it.

The only residual caveat is environmental, not code: the item passes live **only if the dev server has outbound internet to reach `api.pwnedpasswords.com`**. If that egress is blocked, the check fails open (by design) and the item would need a note — the agent will flag that if it happens.

## Root cause (reproduced)

Good instinct, and technically yes — Playwright can screenshot a single element (`element.screenshot()`), so capturing the rendered drawing is easy to do. But let me be straight about whether it's the *right* fix, because we don't actually have a "can't download them" problem — and I don't want to swap in a worse approach to solve something that isn't the fault.

**What I've already proven:** the drawing SVGs **do** download fine — I fetched two directly and got `200 · image/svg+xml · 22 KB / 95 KB`. They're clean **vector** files. So downloading works. The break is somewhere *after* that (the connector not finding them at runtime, or the write/persist step) — the diagnosis running now will say which.

**Trade-off if we screenshotted instead:**
- Today we bring in the **real vector SVG** — crisp at any size, tiny file. A screenshot gives a **raster PNG** — heavier, blurry when scaled, and you have to crop it exactly to the drawing or you catch page chrome. So we'd be trading *down* in quality to fix a download problem we don't have.

**The one scenario where your idea genuinely wins:** if the *separate server-side download* is being blocked in the **prod** environment where Scott & Greg run it (even though the browser can see the image on the page). If that's the real cause, the cleaner fix isn't a screenshot — it's to pull the image **through the browser's own network session** (`page.context().request.get(url)`), which keeps the crisp SVG and uses the same connection that already loaded the page. **Screenshot stays as the last-resort fallback** if even that can't get the bytes.

So: hold the screenshot idea in reserve — it's the right tool only if we find the asset truly can't be retrieved. The re-scrape running now (with the debug line) will tell us in a minute whether it's **extraction**, **the separate fetch**, or **the write**, and I'll route the matching fix through `/implement`. I'll report the second it lands.

I've traced it end to end — this is a real, reproducible defect, and I can tell you exactly why "test works, real doesn't." No live-server poking needed; the code proves it.

## What's happening

There are **two different email paths**, and they read SMTP config from **two different places**:

| | "Send test" button (works) | Onboarding / verification email (silent) |
|---|---|---|
| Code path | [admin.ts:89](apps/api/src/routes/admin.ts#L89) → `smtpConfigFromInput(req.body)` | `sendVerification` → `sendMail` → [smtp.ts:13](apps/api/src/services/smtp.ts#L13) `getSmtpConfig()` |
| Config source | **the values currently typed in the form** | **the saved settings store** (`platformsettings`) |
| On failure | returns the real error to the screen | `sendMailSafe` **swallows it** ([mailer.ts:49](apps/api/src/services/mailer.ts#L49)) |

## The root cause

The **SMTP password never gets saved by the main "Save settings" button.** Look at [Settings.tsx:95](apps/web/src/pages/admin/Settings.tsx#L95):

```js
for (const k of ALL_KEYS) {
  if (isSecret(k.key)) continue;   // ← password is a secret, so it's SKIPPED here
  ...
}
```

The password only persists through a **separate "SMTP password" edit control** ([saveSecret, line 108](apps/web/src/pages/admin/Settings.tsx#L108)). So the natural flow produces exactly your symptom:

1. Admin types host/port/user/from **and** the password into the form.
2. Clicks **Send test** → uses the **typed** password → ✅ works.
3. Clicks **Save settings** → saves everything **except the password** (skipped at line 95).
4. Password is never persisted → `smtp.password` stays empty.
5. Registration fires `sendVerification` → `getSmtpConfig()` reads an **empty password** → `buildTransport` authenticates with `pass: ""` ([smtp.ts:30](apps/api/src/services/smtp.ts#L30)) → **the mail server rejects auth** → `sendMailSafe` swallows the error → **no email, no warning.**

The swallowed failure *is* recorded as an `email_failed` event in the portal — that's the confirming evidence on the live server.

## Two fixes (I'll route through WXKanban `/implement`, not hand-code)

This is a **SCOPE-003 (Global Admin Portal)** defect, with an assist from SCOPE-002 C3 ("a failed send is never swallowed"):

1. **Make Save persist the password** (or make the split obvious) — the primary UX bug. Right now it's a trap.
2. **Surface a saved-config validation warning** so an incomplete SMTP config (host set, password empty) is visible in the portal instead of only silently in the event log — honors SCOPE-002 C3.

## Immediate workaround (fixes it on the live server right now, no deploy)

In the Global Admin Portal → Settings, use the dedicated **"SMTP password"** control to enter and save the password (the separate one, not just "Save settings"). Then register a test tenant — the onboarding email should send. If you can check the portal's event log for `email_failed` entries, that'll confirm the auth-rejection story.

## implement Report — SCOPE-003 (Global Administration Portal)

**Defect:** onboarding/verification email silently not sending on tenant registration; only the SMTP *test* email reaches the server.

**Root cause (confirmed from code):** two email paths, two config sources.
- **"Send test"** exercises the **on-screen form** (`smtpConfigFromInput` — this is intended, FR-007: "test uses the settings just entered, without needing them saved first").
- **Every real send** (`sendVerification`, invitations, password-reset → `mailer.sendMail` → `getSmtpConfig`) reads the **saved settings store only**. SMTP is portal-only (no `SMTP_*` env vars exist anywhere), so an incomplete saved config → `getSmtpConfig()` returns null → `sendMail` throws in prod → `sendMailSafe` **swallows** it to an `email_failed` event nobody sees. Test passes, real sends fail, invisibly — and the read-only password field renders "unset" identically to "saved."

**Fix (frontend-only, no change to any send path):**
| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `apps/web/.../admin/smtp-status.ts` *(new)* | pure `smtpEmailStatus(savedKeys)` — derives status from which `smtp.*` keys actually have a saved row |
| `apps/web/.../admin/Settings.tsx` | green/amber banner in the Email (SMTP) group (green = host+password saved; amber names exactly what's missing); **"Not set"** chip on any secret with no saved row; **"unsaved changes"** note — *Send test uses on-screen values; live email uses saved values* |

**Verification:** web typecheck clean; `smtpEmailStatus` exercised across all four states (both-saved→good; none / host-only / password-only→warning, correct copy); fixed a banner-flash nit (gated on first load). **Not yet UI-verified live** — I'd want a Playwright pass on dev before you rely on it.

```

```

The app was actually built on **PostgreSQL/React** and stores specs **relationally** (`modelspecgroups` + `modelspecfields`), not as JSON. Bottom line: **the core catalogue is built; the gaps are concentrated in multi‑source ingestion, scrape orchestration/monitoring, normalisation/dedup, and mobile offline.**

|---|---|---|

| **F02** Model Master Data | 🟡 Partial | `models` built; specs are **relational, not versioned `SpecsJson`**. ## Design proposal — Screen 1: Catalogue Home / Search

- **Layout** — A search‑first stack: page header → one prominent search bar → a horizontal row of **type quick‑filters** (chips) → result count → a clean responsive card grid. *Rationale: the pack's "easy to follow" comes from one obvious path down the page, not a toolbar of controls.*
- **Hierarchy** — Eye hits the **search bar** first, the **type chips** second, the **grid** third. "Request an addition" demoted to a quiet secondary in the header. *Rationale: browsing is the job; requesting is the exception.*
- **Cards** — 16:9 image area, **make + model** bold, one muted spec line (`type · hp · years`). I **drop the "Published" pill** every card carried — everything a tenant sees is published, so it was pure noise. *Rationale: less repeated chrome = cleaner scan.*
- **Filters** — Type becomes tappable **chips** (All · Excavator · Dozer · Grader · Dump Truck · Loader · Skid‑Steer); Make stays a dropdown on the right. *Rationale: the complaint was complexity; chips read at a glance where dropdowns hide their options.*
- **States** — loading (skeleton cards), empty ("No machines match" + Request CTA), results. Safety‑yellow used *sparingly* — search focus ring, the active chip, the Request button's accent.
- **A11y** — 44px targets, 16px min text (already house rule), chips are real buttons with `aria-pressed`, contrast AA on the yellow‑on‑black pairs.

I dug into the actual code. Here's the straight answer.

## Can a DDES user start/stop scraping *from inside the app* today?
**No.** There is no button, screen, or control anywhere in the app to start, stop, pause, or schedule scraping. A business user at DDES cannot do it.

## What actually exists in the build

**1. A command‑line script — this is the *only* thing that really scrapes.**
`apps/api/src/scrape-ritchiespecs.ts`, run from a terminal by a developer on the server/dev machine:
```bash
npm run scrape:ritchiespecs -w @pbd/api -- construction --limit 20     # start a run
npm run scrape:ritchiespecs -w @pbd/api -- --dry-run                    # count only, writes nothing
```
- It uses a real headless browser (Playwright) to pull from Ritchie Specs.
- It's limited to four hard‑coded cleared categories (Agriculture, Construction, Lifting & Material Handling, Transportation).
- Everything it pulls lands as **candidates** (hidden from tenants until your team approves them on the Candidates tab).
- **To stop it:** there's no stop button — you `Ctrl‑C` the terminal. It also has no scheduler, so it only runs when a person types that command. There's no automatic/recurring scraping.

**2. A dormant admin API endpoint — exists, but does nothing real.**
There's a DDES‑admin‑only `POST /admin/catalogue/ingest` endpoint (and even a web API client method for it), **but** the server is deliberately wired to the `NullRitchieSpecsConnector` — a safe stub that "yields nothing, never throws." The real scraping connector is *intentionally not imported by the API server*. So even if a button called this endpoint, it would return an empty run and scrape nothing. And no UI button calls it anyway.

## Why it's built this way
The code comments say the live in‑app connector was **deferred** "until Scott & Greg supply the cleared category list," with the null stub as the safe default. So the plumbing (endpoint + service) is stubbed in, but the actual in‑app trigger was never finished.

## The bottom line
- **Today:** scraping = a developer running a terminal command; stopping = Ctrl‑C. Not a DDES self‑service capability.
- **What's missing** is exactly the two screens we were just designing: **Source Administration** (turn a source on/off, set schedule) and the **Scrape Job Monitor** (start a run, watch it, stop it, see failures). Those are what would give DDES a real in‑app start/stop — and it's the F03 gap from the Gap Analysis.

Want me to (a) design the **Scrape Job Monitor** next so start/stop/monitor is specced, or (b) hold and just note this as the answer?

# SCOPE‑032 — Catalogue Ingestion Sources & Job Control

**Depends‑On:** SCOPE‑013 (catalogue models/candidates/publish), SCOPE‑008 (permissions), SCOPE‑011 (audit), SCOPE‑012 (retention), SCOPE‑014 (encrypted store for credentials).

**Overview / value:** Give DDES the ability to **configure catalogue data sources and start, stop, schedule and monitor ingestion runs from inside the app** — replacing today's terminal‑only, developer‑run script (and the dormant null‑connector endpoint). Everything ingested stays a **candidate** until approved through the existing SCOPE‑013 review gate. Closes gap‑analysis items **F01 (source registry), F03 (scrape orchestration + monitor)**, and the merge half of **F04/F09**.

**In scope:** source registry (Source Administration), run start/stop/schedule, the Scrape Job Monitor, per‑run + per‑URL audit, source‑priority merge, wiring the real connectors to an in‑app, cancellable, backgrounded job.
**Out of scope:** the publish/approve flow (stays in SCOPE‑013), anything tenant‑facing, mobile.

**Functional requirements**
- **FR‑001 Source registry** — CRUD sources: name, unique code, access method (API | scraped‑web), base URL, description, categories covered, merge priority, schedule, enabled. Retire ≠ delete. DDES‑admin only.
- **FR‑002 Credentials** — per‑source auth (API key / credentials / public), encrypted at rest, never shown plaintext after save; **Test connection** validates without ingesting.
- **FR‑003 Start a run (in‑app)** — DDES starts a run per source (optional category/limit), runs in the background server‑side; results land as **candidates only**.
- **FR‑004 Stop/cancel a run** — DDES can stop a running run; partial candidates kept + marked; ends `cancelled`; one active run per source.
- **FR‑005 Job lifecycle** — queued → running → completed | partial | failed | cancelled; per‑run counts (fetched / created / flagged‑duplicate / failed), timing, started‑by; degrades gracefully, never corrupts published data.
- **FR‑006 Per‑URL run detail** — each item's outcome (ok / duplicate / failed + reason + source ref); powers "view failures" / retry‑failed.
- **FR‑007 Scrape Job Monitor screen** — list runs with live status, Start, Stop, drill‑in to per‑URL detail, auto‑refresh while active.
- **FR‑008 Scheduling** — per source: Manual / Daily / Weekly; scheduled runs use the same candidate flow; pausable.

**#1 (recorded):** two run modes —
- **Initial sweep** — a throttled first full pull that discovers the fastest rate the source tolerates *without blocking us* (adjustable per‑item delay), and is **resumable across days** so a big catalogue can complete over several nights rather than one hammering session.
- **Weekly incremental** — a recurring run in a **00:00–05:00 window**, importing **only new records** (anything already in the catalogue is skipped by the duplicate guard; only genuinely new models become candidates).

**#5 (recorded):** 12‑month run‑log retention.

---

## #2 — Where do the "Verified / Year range / Source / Last‑verified" fields live?

**What they are:** the extra columns Scott's Model Detail shows — the green *Verified – Approved* badge, production **year range** (2015–2022), which **source** supplied the data, and **last‑verified date + by whom**.

**Why it's a separate question from ingestion:** "verified / approved / last‑verified‑by" isn't a scraping mechanic — it's a **human data‑quality workflow on the model record**, and it's really an *extension of SCOPE‑013's* existing candidate→published lifecycle. Ingestion (032) only knows "this came from source X on date Y"; a person deciding "yes, these specs are correct — verified" is a different act.

**The options:**
- **A) Fold into 032** — one build, but it mixes model master‑data + a human verification workflow into a scope that's supposed to be about *running scrapers*. Muddier.
- **B) A separate SCOPE‑033 "Catalogue Model Master Data & Verification"** — owns the new model columns (verified, year‑from/to, source summary, last‑verified) **and** the verification workflow on Model Detail (the *Verified – Approved* panel + *Request Verification*). 032 just writes the source/date provenance; 033 adds the human layer on top.
- **C) Amend SCOPE‑013** — **not possible**; the kit can't cleanly edit an already‑materialised scope (we've hit this before), which is exactly why new model fields need a new scope.

**Recommendation: B (separate SCOPE‑033).** It keeps 032 about start/stop/monitor — *your actual question* — so we can build and ship it independently, and it puts the verification workflow where it belongs. The trade‑off to know: the *Verified badge* and *Year range* on the redesigned screens won't light up until 033 is built, so 033 becomes the prerequisite for those parts of Scott's screens. I'd build **032 first, 033 next.**

## #3 — When two sources disagree, auto‑merge or flag for review?

**The scenario:** once you have more than one source, both might describe "Komatsu WA500" but give different numbers for the same spec (e.g. operating weight 29,000 vs 29,050 kg). Something has to decide which wins.

- **Auto‑merge (priority wins):** each source has a priority number; for a conflicting field the higher‑priority source's value is used automatically, and provenance records which source gave each value. **Fast, no human bottleneck**; risk = silently trusting a wrong value from the "preferred" source.
- **Flag for review:** on disagreement the model is queued for a human to pick. **More accurate**, but creates ongoing review workload.

**The key fact:** with **one source in v1 (see #4), there is nothing to merge** — this only ever triggers once you add a second source.

**Recommendation: auto‑merge by priority + provenance, *plus* a "source conflict" flag** surfaced in the review queue (so a human *can* check disagreements but is never *blocked* by them). We build the priority field + provenance now; because v1 is single‑source it stays dormant until you add source #2 — so you get the mechanism without paying for a review queue you don't yet need.

## #4 — RitchieSpecs only, or also the HeavyEquipmentData API now?

- **RitchieSpecs (scraped):** we **already have a working connector** (the Playwright code the CLI uses). Wiring it into the in‑app job = adding start/stop/monitor/schedule *around code that already works*. Low risk, and it's exactly what your #1 sweep/weekly plan describes.
- **HeavyEquipmentData (API):** we have **no connector, no credentials, and no confirmed subscription/licensing**. Adding it means a new API adapter, credential handling, a **commercial decision + cost**, and testing against their service — net‑new integration plus a purchasing call, not just a build.

**Recommendation: v1 = RitchieSpecs only, but build the source registry as a *pluggable framework*** so adding HeavyEquipmentData (or Lectura, Plant Specs…) later is *config + one adapter*, not a re‑architecture. Reasons: it's the connector that exists and works, it directly delivers your start/stop/weekly‑sweep need, HeavyEquipmentData is gated on a licensing/cost decision you'd need to make first, and the registry keeps source #2 cheap when you're ready. (This matches the gap analysis, where multi‑source was the deferred item.)

---

**So, proposed final shape:** SCOPE‑032 = source registry + initial‑sweep + weekly‑incremental (00:00–05:00, new‑only) + start/stop/monitor, **RitchieSpecs wired**, pluggable for more, auto‑merge+conflict‑flag mechanism (dormant at one source), 12‑month log retention. And a **follow‑on SCOPE‑033** for the model verification/year/source fields that Scott's screens display.

> Why are we at only 93% coverage for Scope-032

**17:38 — Claude:**

Because of **exactly one requirement — FR‑014 (Run‑log retention).**

The coverage metric counts an FR as "covered" only when it has **both** a user scenario **and** a success criterion. All 15 FRs have a success criterion, and 14 also have a scenario. FR‑014 is the lone exception:

- ✅ It **has** a success criterion — **SC11** ("Run records and per‑URL detail older than 12 months are purged; source records persist").
- ❌ It has **no user scenario** — because purging is an **automated background policy**, not something a person does. None of US1–US6 (start a sweep, run the weekly job, stop a run, add a source, resolve a conflict, get refused) naturally exercises "12 months later, the logs get deleted."

So it's **14/15 = 93%**, and the missing 7% is purely that retention is a silent housekeeping job with no human in the loop.

**Is that a problem?** Not really — SC‑only coverage is defensible for a cross‑cutting background policy (SCOPE‑012‑style retention behaves the same way across the app). That's why I flagged it as acceptable rather than a finding.

**But we can make it 100%** cleanly: FR‑014 *does* have an actor — the **ingestion job engine** (already a secondary actor) — so I can add a system‑actor scenario, e.g.:

> **US7 — Run logs age out *(retention, system)*.** Twelve months after a run completes, the scheduled retention job purges that run's records and per‑URL detail; the source and its published candidates are untouched.

That gives FR‑014 a scenario **and** its existing SC11, taking coverage to **15/15 = 100%**.

## What was wrong
Your SMTP host was saved as **`" smtp.mxguardian.net"` with a leading space**. Node's DNS rejected that as a bad name (`queryA EBADNAME`), so every email — Andrew's signup verification and Garth's invite — failed silently and was only recorded as an `email_failed` event. Nothing was actually broken with your mail provider or credentials.

## What I fixed
- Trimmed the whitespace on the SMTP settings → host is now `smtp.mxguardian.net`.
- Verified it **resolves in DNS** (18.206.27.184) and the **mail server responds** on port 2525.
- No API restart needed — the app reads SMTP settings fresh on every send, so the next email uses the corrected host.

## What you need to do (the failed ones won't auto-retry)
1. **Garth's invite:** Members → the pending invitation for `gwhpta@gmail.com` → **Resend**.
2. **Andrew's signup:** have him request a new verification email (or re-invite `andrew.mathieson-blakely@bmcg.net.au`).

## To stop it happening again
The real bug is that the settings screen doesn't trim whitespace on save, so a stray space breaks mail again next time. It's a one-line fix in the settings save path (`btrim` the values). Want me to make that change? (It'd be an edit to `settings.ts` in your working tree — nothing committed or pushed unless you ask.)

That error is a **directory problem, not a real config problem** — nothing's wrong with your `.env`. `--env-file ../.env` is **relative to the folder you run it from**. The error says it looked in `/home/.env`, which means you were sitting in your home directory (`/home/…`) when you ran it, not in the repo's `deploy/` folder. So `../.env` resolved to the wrong place.

Fix: run the commands **from inside the repo's `deploy/` directory**, where `../.env` correctly points at the repo-root `.env`.

**1. Find where the repo is checked out on the dev box** (if you're not sure of the path):
```bash
sudo find / -path '*/deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml' 2>/dev/null
```
That prints something like `/opt/pbd/deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` (or wherever it actually lives — `/root/…`, `/home/<user>/proactive-by-ddes/…`, etc.).

**2. Go to that repo root and confirm the `.env` is there:**
```bash

ls -la .env            # must exist. If it does, you're in the right place.
```

**3. Run the deploy from there:**
```bash
git fetch origin
git checkout dev
git reset --hard origin/dev

cd deploy
ls -la ../.env         # sanity check — this must list the file before you continue
docker compose --env-file ../.env -f docker-compose.prod.yml down -v
./bootstrap.sh
```

The key checks: **`ls -la .env` from the repo root** and **`ls -la ../.env` from `deploy/`** must both show the file before you run the compose commands.

Two possibilities to tell apart:
- **You just ran it from the wrong folder** (most likely, given `/home/.env`) → cd into the repo as above and it works.
- **The `.env` genuinely isn't at the repo root** on this server → that's a different fix (create it from `deploy/.env.production.example`), but since dev.proactive.ddes.app is already live, the file almost certainly exists — you were just in the wrong directory.

## 10:37 — Andrew

> Okay so lets have a look at 1.  SMTP on the dev server so testing shows that the email is being sent out via MXGuardian but it is not being recieved on the receivers side.  I am wondering if we need to look at a more robust solution such as a service like Mailgun

**10:38 — Claude:**

Good question — and "sent OK but never arrives" is almost always a **deliverability** problem, not a config one. The receiving server (Gmail/Outlook) silently drops or junks mail whose sending domain isn't properly authorized (SPF/DKIM/DMARC). Also worth knowing: **MXGuardian is really an inbound spam-filtering service, not a transactional sender** — so your instinct to move is sound. Let me check the DNS for the sending domain first:

<details><summary>Actions taken (1)</summary>

- 10:38 — Ran: Check SPF/DKIM/DMARC deliverability records for ddes.app

</details>

**10:39 — Claude:**

Diagnosis from the DNS — and it points at deliverability, not your app:

- **SPF:** `include:spf.mxguardian.net` ✅ (mxguardian *is* authorized to send as ddes.app)
- **DMARC:** `p=reject` ⚠️ — **strict.** Any mail claiming `@ddes.app` that fails DMARC alignment is **hard-rejected** by Gmail/Outlook, silently from your side.
- **DKIM:** a `default` selector exists, but it belongs to your primary mailbox host — the app's relayed mail almost certainly **isn't DKIM-signed as ddes.app**, and relayed submission mail often doesn't SPF-align either.

So: mxguardian *accepts* the message (your "sent" = the relay hop), but the recipient **rejects it under `p=reject`** because it isn't aligned. That's the classic "sends fine, never arrives." And you're right that **MXGuardian is an inbound spam-filter, not a transactional sender** — you're using it off-label.

**Recommendation: yes, move to a transactional provider** (Mailgun, Postmark, or Amazon SES). That's the robust fix — real deliverability (aligned SPF+DKIM so you pass `p=reject`), plus logs and bounce handling.

The good news, and why it's KISS: **for our app it's a config change, not a code change.** The mailer already reads SMTP settings from the DDES portal, and all three providers offer an SMTP endpoint. So switching is:
1. Create the account, **verify the ddes.app sending domain** (add their SPF include + DKIM records to DNS — this is what actually fixes it),
2. Enter their SMTP host/user/pass/from in the portal → Test.

No rebuild, no spec gate (it's infra/config).

Quick steer if you want one:
- **Postmark** — best transactional deliverability, simplest, ~US$15/mo. My pick for signup/invite mail.
- **Amazon SES** — cheapest (~$0.10/1k) but more setup (leave the sandbox).
- **Mailgun** — fine too; the one you named.

Which do you want to go with? Once you pick and create the account, I'll give you the exact DNS records to add and wire the SMTP settings.

**19:34 — Claude:**

Parked. Here's the *why* — the mechanism behind these false positives:

**The rule:** JS-0067 is DeepSource's port of ESLint's `no-implicit-globals`. That rule exists to catch a real problem in old-style browser scripts: in a plain `<script>`, a top-level `function foo() {}` or `var x` becomes a property of the global `window` object, where any other script can clobber it. The rule says "don't declare things at global scope; wrap them or make them module-scoped."

**Why it's wrong here:** the rule *only makes sense for script files*. In an **ES module** — any file with `import`/`export`, which `App.tsx` has at the top — top-level declarations are **module-scoped by the language itself**. They never touch `window`. ESLint's own docs say the rule is a no-op in modules, and disables itself when the parser is told `sourceType: "module"`.

**So the actual defect is analyzer configuration, not your code:** DeepSource is parsing `App.tsx` as a *script*, not a *module*. When it does that, every top-level `function`/`const` looks like a global declaration, so it fires JS-0067 six times. Point it at ES-module mode and all six vanish with zero code change — because there was never a real global there.

**Why it's parsing as a script:** two possible causes —
1. No `.deepsource.toml` in the repo, so the JS analyzer is on its auto-detected/default parsing mode, which isn't classifying these as modules; or
2. The dashboard analyzer config doesn't set the JS environment/module system.

**19:36 — Claude:**

That DeepSource banner you just pasted is the key to the whole thing — let me tie it in, because it's actually *DeepSource admitting the problem, not your code*.

## What that banner means

> "Since the parent branch doesn't have its own pull request, the baseline analysis may not be accurate. Some of the issues raised might belong to one of the parent branches."

DeepSource shows findings on a PR by **diffing against a baseline** (the parent branch). When the parent branch was never analyzed through its own PR, DeepSource has no clean baseline — so it can't tell *your* new lines from lines that were already there. It then dumps **pre-existing findings onto whoever opens the next PR.** That's exactly what happened with JS-0424: your one-line change got blamed for 8 findings that already existed. The banner is DeepSource telling you it's guessing.

## So what are you actually "doing wrong"? Two setup gaps — not code

**1. DeepSource is unconfigured, so it's both over-strict and mis-baselined.**
- No `.deepsource.toml` in the repo → it runs its *maximally strict default* rule set (including pure-opinion rules like "variable name too small" and "unnecessary fragment") **and** parses your ES modules as scripts (the JS-0067 false positives).
- No clean per-branch baseline → the mis-attribution banner above.
- Both are fixed by configuring it **once**.

**2. Nothing catches the trivial stuff *before* it's pushed.** This is the real workflow gap I just found:
- You *have* eslint installed and a `"lint": "eslint ."` script — but **there's no eslint config file**, so that script does essentially nothing.
- There's **no pre-commit hook** (no husky/lint-staged).
- Result: unused imports, stray fragments, `any`s slip through locally and **DeepSource becomes the first place they're ever seen** — post-push, as a wall of findings. It feels constant because there's no earlier net.

## The honest read

The findings we've hit sort into three buckets, and almost none are "bad code":

| Finding | Bucket | Your fault? |
|---|---|---|
| JS-0067 (globals) | **False positive** (module misparse) | No — config |
| JS-C1002 (short names), JS-0424 (fragment) | **Style opinion** | No — DeepSource strictness |
| JS-0339 (non-null `!`) | Safe pragmatic shortcut | Marginal |
| JS-0356 (unused imports) | **Hygiene residue** from fast iteration | Minor, normal |

You're building fast and iterating — deleting code leaves the odd unused import behind. That's ordinary churn, not sloppiness. The reason it *feels* relentless is that an unconfigured, strict analyzer with a broken baseline is amplifying trivial residue into headline findings.

## The one-time fix (kills ~90% of the noise)

1. **Configure DeepSource once** (`.deepsource.toml`): declare JS as ES modules (ends the JS-0067 class + the baseline weirdness improves once branches flow through PRs), and turn off the pure-style rules you don't care about.
2. **Give eslint a real config + `--fix` on pre-commit**: unused imports and fragments then get auto-removed on *your* machine, before they ever reach a PR. DeepSource ends up with almost nothing to report.

Both are small, SPEC-exempt hygiene setup. Want me to do #1 and #2 on a `feat/` branch so this stops being a recurring tax? (I'll still get your nod on the `.deepsource.toml` analyzer list first, since it overrides your dashboard.)

## 09:47 — Andrew

> What does point 2 Residual, deferred by design mean

**09:47 — Claude:**

"**Residual, deferred by design**" = two CVEs that are still open after all the waves, and I left them open **on purpose** (not by oversight). Here's the plain version:

## Which two
From the DeepSource export, `react-router` has two findings that Wave 1 did **not** clear:
- **CVE-2026-53666** — constructor injection during **SSR hydration**
- **CVE-2026-53669** — open-redirect via a backslash in `<Link>`/`useNavigate`

## Why they're still open ("residual")
Wave 1 took react-router-dom to the newest **6.x** (6.30.6), which fixed the one CVE that had a 6.x patch. These two were **only fixed in React Router 7** (7.18.0). There is no 6.x version that fixes them — the only way to close them is to upgrade to React Router **7**, which is a **major version with breaking API changes** (a real code-migration project, not a one-line bump). So they can't ride along in a dependency-patch wave.

## Why leaving them open is safe ("by design")
Both need conditions your app **doesn't have**:
- **CVE-2026-53666** requires **server-side rendering (SSR)**. Your app is a **Vite single-page app** — it renders in the browser, never on a server. That code path literally doesn't run in your build. DeepSource itself marked it **UNREACHABLE**.
- **CVE-2026-53669** (backslash open-redirect) is also marked UNREACHABLE for your usage.

So the risk of leaving them is effectively nil today, while the cost of fixing them now (a full RR6→RR7 migration + re-testing every route) is high. That trade — real cost vs. zero live exposure — is why the sensible call is to **defer**, not patch.

## What "deferred" commits you to
It's tracked as a **decision to make later**, not forgotten: if/when you do a React Router 7 migration (or if your app ever adds SSR, which would make them reachable), that's when you close them. Until then they sit as a known, accepted, low-risk residual.
